bibl.title: Using direct and indirect measures to study perception without awareness

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: method
span.quote: The proposed approach provides a general conceptual/methodological framework for using the dissociation paradigm in studies directed at establishing unconscious processes.

span.label: perception without awareness
span.quote: Many studies directed at demonstrating perception without awareness have relied on the dissociation paradigm (see Erdelyi, 1985, 1986).

span.label: behavioural-experiment
span.quote: Twenty undergraduate students at the University of Waterloo participated in the experiment.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Instructing an observer to respond on a given stimulus dimension makes them exploit whatever conscious information about that dimension exists, which is why a direct task can never be beaten by an indirect one on conscious information.
span.quote: This assumption is based on the reasonable supposition that instructions directing an observer to respond on the basis of a particular stimulus dimension should optimize the observer's use of conscious information that may be available concerning this dimension.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Apparent direct/indirect dissociations can be manufactured by measuring the two indexes on different stimulus states and displays, so the gap reflects unequal discrimination difficulty rather than unconscious perception.
span.quote: These procedures do not satisfy either Criterion 2 or Criterion 3, because the direct and indirect indexes measured discriminative responding be tween different stimulus states under different display con ditions.

span.label: The empirical conclusion may not generalise beyond the specific display and stimulus parameters used.
span.quote: Although this conclusion may be limited to the display and stimulus parameters used in the present studies

span.label: Because the indirect measure was the less sensitive one, the experiments themselves settle nothing about unconscious perception.
span.quote: Given that the sensitivity of the indirect measure in both studies was less than the sensitivity of the comparable direct measures, the present results are inconclusive with regard to unconscious perception.

span.label: The paper cannot explain why its familiarity/duration correlation runs opposite to Avant's, and leaves that to future work.
span.quote: Clearly, additional studies are required to isolate the critical methodological factors responsible for these different patterns of results.

span.label: The field's results are stated to be inconclusive because it has no agreed measure of its central term, not because the experiments are poor.
span.note: what this limits: the accumulated literature on perception without awareness: the paper states definitive results have been elusive in the absence of consensus on what constitutes an adequate measure of awareness
span.quote: Although the logic underlying this paradigm is relatively straightforward, definitive results have been elusive in the absence of any general consensus as to what consti tutes an adequate measure of awareness.

span.label: Whether the available measures are even comparable to one another is stated to be unknowable without a framework that does not exist.
span.note: what this limits: comparing results across studies that used different awareness measures: the paper states it is impossible to know whether those measures are adequate or comparable
span.quote: However, without a general theoretical framework and sufficient empirical data to guide the selection of measures, it is impossible to know if these different measures of conscious aware ness are either adequate or comparable

span.label: The opposing position is rejected on the ground that the thing it depends on cannot be observed.
span.note: what this limits: any claim that a direct discrimination reflects intentional responding: the paper states an observer's intentions cannot be directly observed or measured
span.quote: The problem with Holender's po sition is that the intentions of an observer cannot be directly observed or measured.

span.label: The paper's own diagnosis is that decades of experimental work could not settle the question because the field had no agreed measure of the thing being denied. An empirical programme is stalled by a definitional gap, and the remedy offered is not a better definition but a weaker assumption - an ordering between two sensitivities rather than a claim that either instrument is complete.
span.quote: Although the logic underlying this paradigm is relatively straightforward, definitive results have been elusive in the absence of any general consensus as to what consti tutes an adequate measure of awareness. We propose an alternative approach that involves com parisons of the relative sensitivity of comparable direct and indirect indexes of perception. The only assumption required by the proposed approach is that the sensitivity of direct discrimina tions to relevant conscious information is greater than or equal to the sensitivity of comparable indirect discriminations.

span.label: dissociation paradigm
span.quote: Many studies directed at demonstrating perception without awareness have relied on the dis sociation paradigm.

span.label: measure of awareness
span.quote: in the absence of any general consensus as to what consti tutes an adequate measure of awareness.

span.label: direct measures
span.quote: is that they provide direct measures of perceptual process ing; that is to say, subjects are explicitly instructed to per form the discriminations of interest.

span.label: exhaustiveness assumption
span.quote: This implied consequence of conscious percep tion can be true only if it is also assumed that direct mea sures provide an exhaustive measure of conscious perceptual experience. If this additional exhaustiveness assumption is not made, then there is no reason to expect that a direct measure of perception will always indicate greater than zero perceptual sensitivity, given conscious perceptual experience.

span.label: null sensitivity
span.quote: This implied consequence of conscious percep tion can be true only if it is also assumed that direct mea sures provide an exhaustive measure of conscious perceptual experience. If this additional exhaustiveness assumption is not made, then there is no reason to expect that a direct measure of perception will always indicate greater than zero perceptual sensitivity, given conscious perceptual experience.

span.label: indirect measure
span.quote: The proposed approach is illustrated through an evaluation of Avant and Thieman's (1985) recent claim that an indirect measure of perception based on judgments of apparent visual duration provides a more sensitive indicator of perception than does a direct measure based on forced-choice recognition. Contrary to this claim, when direct and indirect in dexes are measured under comparable conditions, an indirect measure based on judgments of perceived duration provides a less sensitive index of perceptual processing than do comparable direct measures.

span.label: measure of perception - DIRECT: subjects are explicitly instructed to perform the discriminations of interest, which is what makes the measure direct
span.quote: is that they provide direct measures of perceptual process ing; that is to say, subjects are explicitly instructed to per form the discriminations of interest.

span.label: measure of perception - INDIRECT: one index assumed to indicate availability to awareness, the other assumed to indicate availability of the information regardless of awareness
span.quote: One index is assumed to indicate the availability of stimulus information to awareness or consciousness, and the second is assumed to indicate the availability of stimulus information

span.label: perception without awareness - A LITERATURE BLOCKED BY A DEFINITIONAL GAP RATHER THAN BY DATA: 'definitive results have been elusive IN THE ABSENCE OF ANY GENERAL CONSENSUS AS TO WHAT CONSTITUTES AN ADEQUATE MEASURE OF AWARENESS.' The proposed fix does not settle the definition but MINIMISES what must be assumed - 'THE ONLY ASSUMPTION required by the proposed approach is that the sensitivity of direct discriminations to relevant conscious information is GREATER THAN OR EQUAL TO' that of comparable indirect ones
span.quote: Although the logic underlying this paradigm is relatively straightforward, definitive results have been elusive in the absence of any general consensus as to what consti tutes an adequate measure of awareness. We propose an alternative approach that involves com parisons of the relative sensitivity of comparable direct and indirect indexes of perception. The only assumption required by the proposed approach is that the sensitivity of direct discrimina tions to relevant conscious information is greater than or equal to the sensitivity of comparable indirect discriminations.

span.label: contradicts → Avant and Thieman (1985)
span.quote: One very straightforward implication of the present results is that they provide absolutely no support for Avant and Thieman's (1985) claim that judgment of apparent visual duration constitutes a sensitive measure of unconscious perception.

span.label: contradicts → Avant & Lyman (1975); Avant et al. (1975); Avant & Thieman (1985)
span.quote: On the other hand, the present results are completely inconsistent with the negative relation between stimulus familiarity and perceived duration reported by Avant and his colleagues (Avant & Lyman, 1975; Avant et al., 1975; Avant & Thieman, 1985).

span.label: replicates → the filled-duration illusion (Allan, 1979; Craig, 1973; Goldfarb & Goldstone, 1963)
span.quote: This finding represents a successful replication of the filled duration illusion.

span.label: direct measures —operationalised-as→ measure of awareness
span.note: differs in: WHETHER THE EXHAUSTIVENESS ASSUMPTION IS MADE. Reading a null on a direct measure as an absence of awareness 'can be true ONLY IF it is also assumed that direct measures provide AN EXHAUSTIVE MEASURE of conscious perceptual experience. IF THIS ADDITIONAL EXHAUSTIVENESS ASSUMPTION IS NOT MADE, THEN THERE IS NO REASON TO EXPECT that a direct measure of perception will always indicate greater than zero perceptual sensitivity, given conscious perceptual experience' · strength of the relation: 0.9 — A NULL MEASUREMENT MEANS ABSENCE ONLY IF THE INSTRUMENT IS EXHAUSTIVE, and the assumption is usually implicit - the paper calls it 'another IMPLICIT assumption underlying many recent applications of the dissociation paradigm'. This is the 1988 psychology statement of the problem that a verifier cannot report absence.
span.quote: This implied consequence of conscious percep tion can be true only if it is also assumed that direct mea sures provide an exhaustive measure of conscious perceptual experience. If this additional exhaustiveness assumption is not made, then there is no reason to expect that a direct measure of perception will always indicate greater than zero perceptual sensitivity, given conscious perceptual experience.

span.label: indirect measure —distinct-from→ direct measures
span.note: differs in: WHETHER THE TWO ARE MEASURED UNDER COMPARABLE CONDITIONS. Avant and Thieman (1985) claimed an indirect measure was MORE sensitive than a direct one; 'CONTRARY TO THIS CLAIM, WHEN DIRECT AND INDIRECT INDEXES ARE MEASURED UNDER COMPARABLE CONDITIONS', the indirect measure is LESS sensitive. The ordering of the two instruments reverses on the comparability of the conditions, not on the instruments · strength of the relation: 0.85 — THE PUBLISHED CLAIM AND ITS REVERSAL USE THE SAME TWO MEASURES. What changed is that they were put on comparable footing - the same lesson as measuring candidates within one run rather than across runs.
span.quote: The proposed approach is illustrated through an evaluation of Avant and Thieman's (1985) recent claim that an indirect measure of perception based on judgments of apparent visual duration provides a more sensitive indicator of perception than does a direct measure based on forced-choice recognition. Contrary to this claim, when direct and indirect in dexes are measured under comparable conditions, an indirect measure based on judgments of perceived duration provides a less sensitive index of perceptual processing than do comparable direct measures.

span.label: t-test
span.quote: As expected, filled intervals were judged as longer than blank intervals of the same stimulus duration for both word-blank pairs [t(19) = 12.0, p < .0001] and nonword-blank pairs [t(19) = 9.32, p < .00(1).

span.label: ANOVA
span.quote: To compare the sensitivity of the two tasks directly, we further analyzed the results using a 2 X 2 analysis of vari ance that evaluated both task (i.e., lexical decision vs. duration judgment) and task order (i.e., lexical decision first vs, duration judgment first).

span.label: ANOVA
span.quote: In addition, a 2 x 2 x 2 analysis of variance that evaluated task (i.e., stimulus detection vs. duration judgment), stimulus pairing (i.e., word-blank vs. nonword-blank), and task order (i.e., stimulus detection first vs. duration judgment first) revealed that only the main effect of task was a significant source of variance [F(1,18) = 48.32, P < .001].

span.label: p-value
span.quote: More specifically, words, in general, were judged as longer than nonwords [t(19) = 2.44, p < .05].

span.label: mean
span.quote: The data for Experiment 1 are the mean propor tions of "longer" responses for words and nonwords presented for 50 msec.

span.label: The paper's central deduction is that unconscious perception is established as soon as an indirect measure is absolutely more sensitive to a stimulus dimension than a comparable direct measure.
span.quote: The important implication of the above assumption is that unconscious perception is demonstrated whenever an indirect measure shows greater absolute sensitivity than does a comparable direct measure to a particular stimu lus dimension.

span.label: Because only relative sensitivity matters, the direct measure no longer has to show zero sensitivity, which removes the null-awareness requirement that had blocked the dissociation paradigm.
span.quote: To demonstrate uncon scious perception, it is sufficient to establish that the sen sitivity of the indirect measure is greater than the sensi tivity of a comparable direct measure, even if the sensitivity of the directmeasure is greater than zero.

span.label: Experiment 1 replicated the filled-duration illusion: displays containing a word or a nonword were judged longer than blank displays of identical physical duration.
span.quote: As expected, filled intervals were judged as longer than blank intervals of the same stimulus duration for both word-blank pairs [t(19) = 12.0, p < .0001] and nonword-blank pairs [t(19) = 9.32, p < .00(1).

span.label: At 50 ms, words were judged longer than nonwords, i.e. familiarity and perceived duration were positively related, the opposite of the negative relation Avant and colleagues report.
span.quote: More specifically, words, in general, were judged as longer than nonwords [t(19) = 2.44, p < .05].

span.label: The duration-judgment measure is blind to lexical status at 33 ms exposure, showing no word/nonword difference at all.
span.quote: However, as suggested by an inspection of Table I, when the exposure duration was 33 msec, no significant difference was found between the proportion of "longer" responses for words and nonwords [1(19) < 1].

span.label: Lengthening exposure only strengthens the positive familiarity effect rather than reversing its direction.
span.quote: Considered together, the results of Experiments 1 and 2 demonstrate that increases in exposure duration simply increase the magnitude of the positive relation between stimulus familiarity and perceived duration.

span.label: With display conditions equated, the direct lexical decision was more sensitive to lexical status than the indirect duration judgment at 33 ms.
span.quote: Only the main effect of task was significant [F(l,38) = 5.10, P < .05], in dicating that performance on the lexical decision task was significantly better than performance on the duration judg ment task.

span.label: The same ordering held for stimulus detection in Experiment 4, so on both dimensions the direct measure beat the comparable indirect duration measure and Avant and Thieman's claim was not supported.
span.quote: Given the greater sensitivity of the detection measure, the present results support the same conclusion as the results of Experiment 3; namely, a direct measure provides a more sensitive index of perception than does a comparable indirect measure based on judgments of per ceived temporal duration.

span.label: indirect measure of perception
span.quote: Conversely, if the discriminative response is not part of the task definition, it should be considered an indirect measure of perception.

span.label: dissociation paradigm
span.quote: The basic logic un derlying this paradigm is that perception without aware ness can be demonstrated via a dissociation between two indexes of perceptual processing.

span.label: exclusiveness assumption
span.quote: This ex clusiveness assumption implies that a sufficient condition for demonstrating perception with awareness is any evi dence indicating that a direct measure shows greater than zero sensitivity.

span.label: exhaustiveness assumption
span.quote: This implied consequence of conscious percep tion can be true only if it is also assumed that direct mea sures provide an exhaustive measure of conscious perceptual experience.

span.label: the single working assumption of the proposed relative-sensitivity approach
span.term: the single working assumption of the proposed relative-sensitivity approach
span.quote: The sensitivity of a direct discrimination is assumed to be greater than or equal to the sensitivity of a com parable indirect discrimination to conscious, task relevant information.

span.label: filled-duration illusion
span.quote: One phenomenon, com monly referred to as the filled-duration illusion, is that filled intervals are judged as longer thanempty intervals of the same temporal duration (e.g., Allan, 1979; Craig, 1973; Goldfarb & Goldstone, 1963).

span.label: exposure duration of the stimulus displays
span.term: exposure duration of the stimulus displays
span.quote: On 144 trials, each stimulus display was presented for 33 msec, whereas on the remaining 144 trials, each display was presented for 67 msec.

span.label: stimulus familiarity (word vs. nonword)
span.quote: In the present study, stimulus familiarity was based on a wordlnonword distinction, and a comparative judgment task was used to measure perceived duration.

span.label: task instruction (direct lexical/detection decision vs. indirect duration judgment)
span.term: task instruction (direct lexical/detection decision vs. indirect duration judgment)
span.quote: In addition, depending on which condition was being tested in the session, the subjects were instructed to decide either "which flash was longer in duration" or "which flash contained a word."

span.label: proportion of "longer" responses
span.quote: The data for Experiment 1 are the mean propor tions of "longer" responses for words and nonwords presented for 50 msec.

span.label: order of the two decision tasks across sessions
span.term: order of the two decision tasks across sessions
span.quote: Half of the subjects made "duration" decisions in the first session and "word" decisions in the second session, whereas the order of de cisions across sessions was reversed for the remaining subjects.

span.label: display/presentation conditions
span.quote: All stimulus displays were presented for 33 msec under presen tation conditions that were exactly the same as those used in Experiments I and 2.

span.label: t(19) = 12.0, p < .0001 — size of the filled-duration effect for word-blank pairs in Experiment 1
span.quote: As expected, filled intervals were judged as longer than blank intervals of the same stimulus duration for both word-blank pairs [t(19) = 12.0, p < .0001] and nonword-blank pairs [t(19) = 9.32, p < .00(1).

span.label: F(l,38) = 5.10, P < .05 — the Experiment 3 main effect of task showing lexical decision outperformed duration judgment
span.quote: Only the main effect of task was significant [F(l,38) = 5.10, P < .05], in dicating that performance on the lexical decision task was significantly better than performance on the duration judg ment task.

span.label: F(1,18) = 48.32, P < .001 — the Experiment 4 main effect of task, detection versus duration judgment
span.quote: In addition, a 2 x 2 x 2 analysis of variance that evaluated task (i.e., stimulus detection vs. duration judgment), stimulus pairing (i.e., word-blank vs. nonword-blank), and task order (i.e., stimulus detection first vs. duration judgment first) revealed that only the main effect of task was a significant source of variance [F(1,18) = 48.32, P < .001].

span.label: t(39) = 3.23, p < .01 — Experiment 3 direct lexical decision accuracy above chance at 33 ms exposure
span.quote: accuracy of direct lexical decisions in the present experiment was significantly better than chance [t(39) = 3.23, p < .01].

span.label: 60% — accuracy of the indirect preference measure in Kunst-Wilson and Zajonc, against 48% for the direct recognition test
span.quote: Performance on the indirect preference measure was 60% correct, whereas perfor mance on the direct recognition test approximated a chance level of accuracy (48%).

span.label: Twenty — number of undergraduate subjects run in Experiment 1 (and again in Experiments 2 and 4)
span.quote: Twenty undergraduate students at the University of Waterloo participated in the experiment.
